opus-5.5.text:
Chomsky's argument, as I understand it, is roughly this: a good scientific theory of human language should explain not just what humans *can* learn but also what they *can't*. Human languages share certain structural properties, and there are conceivable languages, which he and others have called "impossible languages," that no child would ever acquire naturally. One classic example is a rule that depends on linear word position rather than hierarchical structure, like forming a question by moving the third word to the front. Humans just don't build grammars that way.

So the critique is that if large language models can learn possible and impossible languages equally well, then they aren't telling us anything about the human language faculty. A system that can learn anything explains nothing about why humans learn what they do. Chomsky has made that point quite forcefully in op-eds and interviews, saying these models are essentially as good at learning impossible languages as possible ones, so they can't be a theory of language.

What struck me was that this was mostly asserted rather than tested. It's an empirical claim, so that was really the motivation for our paper, "Mission: Impossible Language Models." We built a set of synthetic impossible languages by systematically altering English data. Some were extreme, like randomly shuffling the words in each sentence. Others were more subtle, like reversing sentences or introducing count-based grammar rules, for instance marking verb agreement with a token placed a fixed number of words after the verb instead of attached to the verb itself. Then we trained GPT-2-style models on each and compared how efficiently they learned.

We found that the models do struggle with the impossible languages compared to natural English. The random shuffles were hardest, and even the subtler count-based rules were learned less efficiently. So the strong version of the claim, that these models learn everything equally well, doesn't really hold up.

I'd stress, though, that this doesn't mean language models are perfect models of human cognition. They're trained on far more data than any child sees, and their inductive biases come from things like the transformer architecture and the training setup, not necessarily from anything humanlike. But I see this as an opening rather than a dismissal. Instead of debating in the abstract whether these models are relevant to linguistics, we can run controlled experiments and ask which inductive biases they have, how those compare to humans, and what architectural changes would bring them closer. In that sense language models can be tools for testing linguistic hypotheses, which is a much more productive position than writing them off entirely.

r001.rationale: The response explains that Chomsky views models as able to learn impossible languages that humans do not naturally acquire, making their learning ability too broad to explain human linguistic behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that actually motivated a lot of the work I did on impossible languages. The argument, as I understand it, goes something like this: Chomsky and some of his co-authors have claimed that large language models are essentially too powerful to be interesting as models of human language. The idea is that if you gave a language model an impossible language, meaning a language that no human could ever naturally acquire, it would learn it just as easily as it learns English or Japanese or any other natural language. And if that's true, then the model isn't really telling us anything about the human language faculty. It's not constrained in the ways humans are constrained, so it's just a general-purpose pattern learner, and the fact that it happens to learn English is sort of incidental.

What struck me about the argument is that it was being made as a kind of a priori claim. It was stated as something that was obviously true, but nobody had actually tested it. And it's a very testable claim. So the natural question for me was, well, what happens if we actually do give language models impossible languages? Do they really learn them just as well as natural languages?

So that's what we did. We constructed a set of synthetic impossible languages by taking English and perturbing it in various ways. Some of these were pretty drastic, like randomly shuffling the words in a sentence, or reversing the entire sentence. Others were more subtle, like inserting a token at a specific position, or having verb agreement depend on counting words rather than on the hierarchical structure of the sentence. And then we trained GPT-2-style models from scratch on each of these languages and compared how well they learned them relative to regular English.

And what we found is that the models do not learn impossible languages as easily. English was learned most efficiently, and the more impossible the language got, the harder it was for the model to learn. The shuffled languages were the hardest, and the ones with these count-based rules were somewhere in between, but still worse than English. So there does seem to be some inductive bias in these models that favors natural-language-like structure, even though they're not explicitly built with any linguistic knowledge.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think this fully settles the question. GPT-2 is not a human child, and the way it learns is very different from how children acquire language. But I think the result does push back on the strong form of Chomsky's argument. It's not the case that these models are indifferent to the structure of what they're learning. There's something about natural language that they find easier, and I think that's genuinely interesting and worth understanding, rather than dismissing out of hand.

r001.rationale: The response explains that Chomsky’s critique sees language models as too powerful and unconstrained by human limits, so their ability to learn even impossible languages makes them poor models of human language.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that the criticism is about what language models are capable of learning, rather than whether they can learn human language. Chomsky’s view is that humans have innate constraints on the kinds of languages we can acquire. So a theory of human language needs to explain both the languages that are possible and the ones that are impossible for us to learn naturally.

A language model, on the other hand, might learn English, but it might also learn a system that violates those proposed constraints. From that perspective, successfully learning English doesn’t necessarily tell us much about human language acquisition, because the model can also learn things that humans supposedly couldn’t.

I think that raises a useful empirical question: Are language models actually equally good at learning all these different systems? Being able to learn something at all isn’t the same as having a preference for it. If models learn human languages more easily than these supposedly impossible languages, then their learning biases may still tell us something relevant about human language—even if their capabilities extend beyond ours.

r001.rationale: The response explains that models can learn systems humans supposedly cannot acquire naturally, so their learning capabilities extend beyond human linguistic constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I understand his argument is that learning human language isn’t, by itself, enough to make something a good model of how humans learn language. You also have to explain what humans can’t learn, or what kinds of languages they wouldn’t naturally acquire.

On Chomsky’s view, humans have innate constraints that restrict the space of possible languages. Language models, by contrast, might learn both human languages and systems that violate those constraints. So his criticism is that they’re too flexible: if they can learn anything, their success on English doesn’t necessarily tell us why human language has the particular structure it does.

I think that raises an interesting empirical question, though. Can these models really learn all those different kinds of languages equally well? Being able to learn something doesn’t mean you have no preferences or biases. Looking at which structures models learn more easily could help us understand whether any of their learning biases line up with ours.

r001.rationale: The response says models may learn systems that violate innate human constraints and are therefore “too flexible” to explain which language structures humans naturally acquire.
